stimuli.title: Pepsin and pH
stimuli.html:
Pepsin is a protein-digesting enzyme made by cells in the stomach lining. A student wanted to know how acidity affects how well pepsin works. She filled six narrow glass tubes with cooked egg white, which is mostly protein, so that each tube held a column of egg white exactly 30 mm long.

She placed each tube in a beaker holding 10 mL of solution. Tubes 1–5 were placed in pepsin solutions of the same concentration that had been adjusted to different pH values. Tube 6 was placed in a pH 2 solution containing pepsin that had first been boiled for 10 minutes. All six beakers were kept in a water bath at 37 °C (body temperature) for 24 hours. She then measured how many millimeters of egg white had been digested away from the open ends of each tube.

TubeSolutionpHEgg white digested (mm)
1Pepsin16.5
2Pepsin29.0
3Pepsin36.0
4Pepsin51.5
5Pepsin70.0
6Boiled pepsin20.0

The inside of the human stomach normally has a pH between about 1.5 and 3.5.

stimuli.title: The Small Intestine's Inner Surface
stimuli.html:
Most digested nutrients enter the blood through the wall of the small intestine. In an adult, the small intestine is a coiled tube about 6 meters long and only about 2.5 centimeters wide. If its inner wall were smooth, it would offer a fairly small surface for nutrients to pass through.

Instead, the inner wall is folded, and the folds are covered with millions of tiny, finger-shaped projections called villi (singular: villus). Each villus is in turn covered with cells whose outer surfaces carry even smaller projections called microvilli. Together, the folds, villi, and microvilli multiply the surface area of the inner wall many times over; scientists estimate the total absorbing surface of an adult's small intestine at roughly 30 square meters.

Inside each villus is a network of tiny blood vessels called capillaries. Sugars from digested carbohydrates and amino acids from digested proteins pass through the thin wall of the villus into these capillaries and are carried away in the blood. Digested fats enter a small lymph vessel in the center of the villus instead.

In celiac disease, a person's immune system reacts to gluten, a protein found in wheat, barley, and rye. When the person eats gluten, the immune reaction damages the lining of the small intestine, and the villi become shortened and flattened. Most people with celiac disease recover healthy villi after they remove gluten from their diet.

stimuli.title: Digesting Milk Sugar as an Adult
stimuli.html:
Milk contains a sugar called lactose. To absorb it, the body must first break lactose into two smaller sugars, glucose and galactose. This reaction is carried out by the enzyme lactase, which is made by cells lining the small intestine.

Nearly all babies produce lactase. In most mammals, and in many people, lactase production drops sharply after early childhood. Adults with low lactase may have bloating and cramps after consuming large amounts of milk. In some human populations, however, many adults keep making lactase throughout life, a trait called lactase persistence.

Lactase persistence is controlled mainly by one gene. The allele for lactase persistence (L) is dominant over the allele for low adult lactase (l).

The table compares two hypothetical populations.

PopulationHistoryAdults with lactase persistence
Population ARaised cattle and goats and drank their milk for thousands of yearsAbout 90%
Population BDid not keep milk-producing animals until recent timesAbout 10%

stimuli.title: Bile and Fat Digestion
stimuli.html:
The enzyme lipase breaks fat molecules into fatty acids and glycerol. Because fatty acids are acids, the pH of a mixture drops as lipase digests fat. Bile, made by the liver and stored in the gallbladder, contains bile salts.

A student set up four test tubes. Each tube held 5 mL of whole milk (which contains fat) and a small amount of a mild base, so every tube started at pH 8.0. The student then added the substances listed below. Whenever a tube did not receive lipase or bile salts, an equal volume of water was added in its place so that every tube held the same total volume. All tubes were kept at 37 °C, and the pH of each was measured after 10 minutes.

TubeAdded to the milkpH at startpH after 10 minutes
ALipase + bile salts8.06.4
BLipase + water8.07.2
CBile salts + water8.08.0
DWater only8.08.0

stimuli.title: A Lunch Log
stimuli.html:
A student recorded the nutrients in one lunch. Food energy is measured in Calories (with a capital C). Each gram of carbohydrate or protein supplies about 4 Calories, and each gram of fat supplies about 9 Calories.

FoodCarbohydrate (g)Protein (g)Fat (g)Calories
Turkey sandwich402512?
Apple2500100

stimuli.title: Measuring the Energy in Food
stimuli.html:
A class measured the energy stored in four snack foods. For each food, a student stuck a 1.0 g sample on a pin, set it on fire, and held it under a small metal can containing 50 g of water. When the sample stopped burning, the student recorded the final temperature of the water.

Food (1.0 g)Starting water temperature (°C)Final water temperature (°C)
Walnut21.061.0
Peanut21.055.0
Popcorn22.037.0
Marshmallow21.533.5

The heat absorbed by the water can be found with Q = mcΔT, where Q is heat in joules (J), m is the mass of the water in grams, c is the specific heat of water (4.18 J/g·°C), and ΔT is the change in temperature in °C.

Walnuts and peanuts are high in fat. Popcorn and marshmallows are made mostly of carbohydrate.

stimuli.title: Testing Antacids
stimuli.html:
Heartburn happens when acid from the stomach moves up into the esophagus. Antacid tablets contain bases that neutralize hydrochloric acid (HCl), the main acid in the stomach. A student compared three brands of antacid.

She poured 100 mL of a dilute hydrochloric acid solution with a pH of 1.5 into each of three beakers. She crushed 1.0 g of one brand of tablet into each beaker, stirred for the same length of time, and measured the pH after 5 minutes.

BrandMain active ingredientpH after 5 minutes
Brand XCalcium carbonate3.5
Brand YMagnesium hydroxide6.8
Brand ZAluminum hydroxide2.2

On the pH scale, a solution with a pH of 7 is neutral. Each decrease of 1 pH unit means the solution is 10 times more acidic.

stimuli.title: Model Buildings on a Shake Table
stimuli.html:
Engineers sometimes place buildings on thick rubber-and-steel pads, called base isolators, so that the ground can move without carrying the whole building with it. A class tested this idea with model buildings.

The class built two identical four-story model buildings from the same wood and glue. Model A was bolted directly to a shake table, a platform that a motor moves back and forth to imitate earthquake shaking. Model B was bolted to four rubber pads, which were attached to the same shake table. At each shaking level, the class shook the table for 20 seconds and used a video recording to measure the greatest side-to-side sway of each model's top floor. They ran three trials at each level and calculated the mean.

Shaking levelModel A mean sway (cm)Model B mean sway (cm)
Low1.20.6
Medium2.51.1
High4.42.0

stimuli.title: Locating an Earthquake
stimuli.html:
An earthquake sends out several kinds of seismic waves. Primary waves (P waves) travel fastest, so they reach a recording station first. Secondary waves (S waves) travel more slowly and arrive later. The farther a station is from the earthquake, the longer the gap between the arrival of the P waves and the arrival of the S waves.

In the region described here, assume P waves travel at 6 km/s and S waves travel at 3 km/s. Under these conditions, the distance from a station to the earthquake, in kilometers, equals 6 × the S–P lag time in seconds.

Four seismic stations recorded the same earthquake.

StationP waves arrivedS waves arrived
North10:15:2010:15:40
East10:15:1010:15:20
South10:15:3510:16:10
West10:15:2510:15:50

Times are given as hours:minutes:seconds.

stimuli.title: Earthquake Magnitude and Ground Failure
stimuli.html:
Seismologists describe the size of an earthquake with a magnitude number. The scale is logarithmic. For each increase of 1.0 in magnitude, the largest ground motion recorded on a seismogram (the wave amplitude) is about 10 times greater, and the energy released is about 32 times greater.

The damage an earthquake causes depends on more than its magnitude. Distance from the earthquake, building design, and the ground beneath a structure all matter. One serious hazard is liquefaction. When loose, sandy soil is soaked with water, strong shaking can push the water pressure between the sand grains so high that the grains lose contact with one another. For a short time, the soil behaves like a thick liquid. Buildings resting on it can tilt or sink, and buried pipes can float upward. Firm bedrock and dry, tightly packed soil do not liquefy.

items.prompt: In Tubes 1 through 5, which variable did the student deliberately change?
options: The pH of the pepsin solution
The length of egg white digested
The temperature of the water bath
The concentration of pepsin
items.explain:
The independent variable is the one the experimenter changes on purpose. Tubes 1–5 were set to pH 1, 2, 3, 5, and 7, so pH is the independent variable.

The length of egg white digested is the dependent variable (what she measured). The temperature (37 °C) and the pepsin concentration were kept the same, so they are controlled variables.
why: The length digested is what she measured (the dependent variable), not what she changed on purpose. She changed the pH: 1, 2, 3, 5, and 7.
All beakers were kept at 37 °C, so temperature was held constant (a controlled variable).
The passage says Tubes 1–5 used pepsin solutions "of the same concentration," so concentration was controlled, not changed.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the data?
options: Pepsin digests more protein as the pH rises toward neutral.
Pepsin works best in strongly acidic conditions similar to those inside the stomach.
Pepsin digests protein equally well at every pH from 1 to 7.
Pepsin works best at pH 7, the pH of pure water.
items.explain:
Digestion peaked at pH 2 (9.0 mm) and dropped on both sides: 6.5 mm at pH 1, 6.0 mm at pH 3, 1.5 mm at pH 5, and 0.0 mm at pH 7. The passage states the stomach's pH is about 1.5–3.5, so pepsin works best in strongly acidic conditions like the stomach's.

Digestion fell, not rose, as pH moved toward 7, and at pH 7 no egg white was digested at all.
why: Digestion fell, not rose, as pH moved toward neutral: 9.0 mm at pH 2 but 1.5 mm at pH 5 and 0.0 mm at pH 7.
The amounts ranged from 9.0 mm to 0.0 mm, so pepsin did not work equally well at every pH.
At pH 7 no egg white was digested (0.0 mm). Digestion peaked at pH 2.

items.prompt:
Complete the statements about the experiment.

Pepsin is a(n) {{0}} that speeds up the breakdown of {{1}} into smaller pieces. Because no egg white was digested in Tube 6, the results show that the digestion in Tube 2 was caused by {{2}}.

options: enzyme
hormone
vitamin
mineral
why: A hormone is a chemical messenger carried in the blood. Pepsin speeds up a reaction, which makes it an enzyme.
Vitamins are nutrients the body needs in small amounts; they do not digest protein. Pepsin is an enzyme.
Minerals are elements such as calcium and iron. Pepsin is a protein that speeds up a reaction: an enzyme.

options: starches
proteins
fats
fiber
why: The passage calls pepsin a protein-digesting enzyme, and egg white is mostly protein. Starches are broken down by amylase.
Fats are broken down by lipase. Pepsin is protein-digesting, and egg white is mostly protein.
Fiber is not broken down by human enzymes. Pepsin digests proteins.

options: the acid alone
the warm temperature
active pepsin
the glass tube
why: Tube 6 had the same acid (pH 2) as Tube 2 but digested 0.0 mm, so acid alone does not digest the egg white.
Tube 6 was kept at the same 37 °C and digested nothing, so warmth alone did not cause digestion.
Every tube used the same kind of glass tube, including Tube 6, which digested nothing. The only difference was boiled pepsin.

items.explain:
Pepsin is an enzyme, a protein that speeds up a chemical reaction. The passage says it is protein-digesting, and egg white is mostly protein, so it breaks down proteins.

Tube 6 had the same pH (2), temperature, and egg white as Tube 2; the only difference was that its pepsin had been boiled, which destroys the enzyme's shape. Tube 6 digested 0.0 mm, so the acid and warmth alone did nothing. The digestion in Tube 2 must have been caused by active pepsin.

items.prompt:
Which variables were kept the same in Tubes 1 through 5 so that the test would be fair?

Select two answers.
options: The temperature of the solutions
The pH of the solutions
The amount of egg white digested
The concentration of pepsin
The amount of acid added to each solution
items.explain:
The passage says all beakers were kept at 37 °C and that Tubes 1–5 used pepsin solutions of the same concentration. Those are controlled variables.

The pH was changed on purpose (independent variable), and the amount digested was measured (dependent variable). The amount of acid added had to differ from tube to tube in order to set the different pH values, so it was not kept the same.
why: pH was changed on purpose from tube to tube; it is the independent variable.
The amount digested was the result being measured (dependent variable), and it differed among tubes.
Different amounts of acid were needed to reach different pH values, so this was not kept the same.

items.prompt: According to the passage, how do villi and microvilli help the small intestine do its job?
options: They produce the enzymes that break proteins into amino acids.
They push food along the intestine with waves of muscle contraction.
They store digested fats until the body needs them.
They greatly increase the surface area through which nutrients are absorbed.
items.explain:
The passage says the folds, villi, and microvilli “multiply the surface area of the inner wall many times over,” to about 30 square meters. More surface means more area through which nutrients can be absorbed into the blood and lymph.

The passage does not say villi make enzymes or move food. Digested fats pass into a lymph vessel inside each villus; they are carried away, not stored there.
why: The passage does not say villi make enzymes. It says the folds, villi, and microvilli "multiply the surface area."
Moving food along is done by muscle contractions, which the passage does not assign to villi. Villi increase the absorbing surface.
Digested fats enter a lymph vessel in each villus and are carried away; the villi do not store them.

items.prompt: A person with celiac disease has not yet been diagnosed and continues to eat bread every day. Based on the passage, which problem is this person most likely to develop?
options: Poor absorption of nutrients, even when eating enough food
An inability to chew and swallow food
Too much stomach acid, causing protein to be digested too quickly
A shortage of gluten in the blood
items.explain:
Bread contains gluten. In celiac disease, eating gluten causes the villi to become shortened and flattened. Flattened villi mean much less surface area, so fewer nutrients can be absorbed, even if the person eats plenty of food.

Celiac disease affects the lining of the small intestine, not chewing, swallowing, or stomach acid. Gluten is the trigger of the reaction; the body does not need it in the blood.
why: Celiac disease damages the lining of the small intestine, not the mouth or throat, so chewing and swallowing are not affected.
The passage says nothing about stomach acid in celiac disease. The damage is to the villi of the small intestine.
Gluten is the trigger of the immune reaction; the body does not need gluten in the blood. The problem is flattened villi and poor absorption.

items.prompt: A man who is heterozygous for lactase persistence (Ll) has children with a woman who has low adult lactase (ll). What percent of their children are expected to have lactase persistence? Enter a whole number.
items.explain:
Set up the cross Ll × ll:

Ll
lLlll
lLlll

L is dominant, so every child with at least one L (the Ll boxes) has lactase persistence. That is 2 of 4 boxes: 2 ÷ 4 = 50%.

Answering 25% treats this like a cross of two heterozygous parents. Answering 75% counts the dominant phenotype from an Ll × Ll cross, which is not this cross.

mistakes.why: 25% is the share of ll children from an Ll × Ll cross. Here only one parent carries L: Ll × ll gives 2 Ll and 2 ll, so 50% have lactase persistence.
75% is the dominant share from two heterozygous parents (Ll × Ll). The mother is ll, so half the boxes are Ll: 50%.
Not every child gets the father's L allele. He is Ll, so half his sperm carry l, and those children are ll: 50% have lactase persistence.

items.prompt: Which explanation best accounts for the difference between Population A and Population B?
options: Drinking milk as adults caused people in Population A to change their own genes, and they passed the changes to their children.
People in Population B chose not to inherit the L allele because they did not need it.
In Population A, adults who could digest milk got extra nutrition, so they tended to survive and have more children, and the L allele became more common over many generations.
The L allele appeared in Population A only after its people began drinking milk.
items.explain:
This is natural selection. Where milk was available, adults carrying L could use it as a food source, giving them a survival and reproductive advantage. Over thousands of years, they passed L to more offspring, so the allele became common (about 90% of adults).

Using a body part or food during life does not rewrite a person's genes, and individuals cannot choose which alleles they inherit. Mutations arise randomly; the environment (dairy herding) changes how often an existing allele is passed on, not whether it appears.
why: Using a food during life does not change a person's genes, so acquired changes cannot be passed on. The L allele became common through natural selection.
Individuals cannot choose which alleles they inherit. Population B lacked the selection pressure that made L common in Population A.
Mutations arise randomly; dairying did not create the L allele. It changed how often an existing allele was passed on.

items.prompt: Which two tubes should be compared to show that bile salts by themselves do not chemically break down fat?
options: Tube A and Tube B
Tube C and Tube D
Tube A and Tube C
Tube B and Tube D
items.explain:
Tube C (bile salts, no lipase) and Tube D (water only) differ only in the presence of bile salts. Both stayed at pH 8.0, so no fatty acids were produced. Comparing C and D shows that bile salts alone do not break fat into fatty acids.

Tubes A and B both contain lipase, so that comparison shows what bile adds to lipase. Tubes A and C differ in lipase, and B and D differ in lipase, so those comparisons test lipase, not bile alone.
why: Tubes A and B both contain lipase, so comparing them shows what bile salts add to lipase, not what bile does alone.
Tubes A and C differ in lipase (A has it, C does not), so the comparison tests lipase, not bile alone.
Tubes B and D differ in lipase, not bile salts. To test bile alone, compare C (bile salts) with D (water only).

items.skill: Path of food through the digestive system
items.prompt: Put the organs in the order that food passes through them, from the moment it is eaten. Drag each organ into the correct position.
items.explain:
Food enters the mouth (1st), is swallowed down the esophagus (2nd), is churned with acid and pepsin in the stomach (3rd), is digested further and absorbed in the small intestine (4th), and leftover material passes into the large intestine (5th), where water is absorbed.

A common mistake is placing the large intestine before the small intestine because of its name; “large” refers to its width, and it comes last.
items.why: The most common error is placing the large intestine before the small intestine because of its name. "Large" refers to its width; food passes mouth, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, and large intestine last.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the results of all four tubes?
options: Bile salts break down fat without the help of lipase.
Lipase cannot digest any fat unless bile salts are present.
Bile salts digest fat by raising the pH of the mixture.
Lipase digests fat, and bile salts make lipase digest fat faster.
items.explain:
Tube B (lipase only) dropped from 8.0 to 7.2, so lipase digests fat on its own. Tube A (lipase + bile) dropped further, to 6.4, in the same 10 minutes, so bile salts speed up fat digestion by lipase. (Bile breaks large fat droplets into tiny ones, giving lipase more surface to work on.)

Tube C shows bile alone causes no pH change, and Tube B shows lipase works without bile. Bile did not raise the pH in any tube.
why: Tube C (bile salts without lipase) stayed at pH 8.0, so bile alone did not break down fat.
Tube B (lipase without bile) dropped from 8.0 to 7.2, so lipase digested some fat on its own.
Bile did not raise the pH in any tube. Tube C stayed at 8.0, and the pH dropped only where lipase was present.

items.prompt: Using the information in the passage, how many Calories does the turkey sandwich supply? Enter a whole number.
items.explain:
Multiply each nutrient's grams by its Calories per gram, then add.

Carbohydrate: 40 g × 4 = 160 Calories
Protein: 25 g × 4 = 100 Calories
Fat: 12 g × 9 = 108 Calories
Total: 160 + 100 + 108 = 368 Calories

A common error is using 4 Calories per gram for fat: 160 + 100 + 48 = 308. Fat supplies 9 Calories per gram.

mistakes.why: You used 4 Calories per gram for fat. Fat supplies 9 Calories per gram: 12 × 9 = 108, so 160 + 100 + 108 = 368.
77 is the total grams of nutrients (40 + 25 + 12), not Calories. Multiply each by its Calories per gram and add: 368.
468 includes the apple's 100 Calories. The question asks only about the sandwich: 368.

items.prompt: About what percent of the Calories in the whole lunch (sandwich and apple) come from fat?
items.explain:
Calories from fat: 12 g × 9 = 108 Calories (the apple has no fat).

Total lunch Calories: 368 (sandwich) + 100 (apple) = 468 Calories.

108 ÷ 468 ≈ 0.231 = about 23%.

29% is the fat share of the sandwich alone (108 ÷ 368). 12% compares grams of fat to grams of all nutrients (12 ÷ 102), not Calories. 3% divides grams of fat by Calories (12 ÷ 468).
why: You divided grams of fat by Calories (12 ÷ 468). Convert fat to Calories first: 12 × 9 = 108, and 108 ÷ 468 ≈ 23%.
You compared grams of fat with grams of all nutrients (12 ÷ 102). The question asks about Calories: 108 ÷ 468 ≈ 23%.
29% is the fat share of the sandwich alone (108 ÷ 368). The whole lunch includes the apple's 100 Calories: 108 ÷ 468 ≈ 23%.

items.prompt: In chemical digestion, food molecules are changed into different, smaller molecules. Click the sentence that describes chemical digestion.
spans: Teeth cut and grind food into smaller pieces.
Waves of muscle contraction push swallowed food down the esophagus.
Muscles in the stomach wall churn food and mix it with gastric juice.
Amylase in saliva breaks starch molecules into smaller sugar molecules.
Bile from the liver breaks large fat droplets into many tiny droplets without changing the fat molecules.
items.explain:
Only the amylase sentence describes molecules being changed into new, smaller molecules: starch is broken into sugars by an enzyme. That is chemical digestion.

Chewing and churning break food into smaller pieces without changing its molecules (mechanical digestion). Muscle waves in the esophagus only move food. Bile breaks fat into smaller droplets, but the sentence states the fat molecules themselves are unchanged, so this is a physical change, not chemical digestion.
items.why: The most common wrong click is the bile sentence, because it mentions breaking down fat. That sentence says the fat molecules are unchanged, so it is a physical change; only amylase breaking starch into sugar makes new molecules.

items.prompt: Use Q = mcΔT to find how much heat, in joules, the water absorbed when the peanut sample burned. Enter a whole number.
items.explain:
ΔT = 55.0 − 21.0 = 34.0 °C

Q = m × c × ΔT
Q = 50 g × 4.18 J/g·°C × 34.0 °C
50 × 4.18 = 209
209 × 34.0 = 7,106 J

A common error is using the final temperature (55.0 °C) instead of the change: 209 × 55.0 = 11,495 J, which is too large.

mistakes.why: You used the final temperature (55.0 °C) instead of the change. ΔT = 55.0 − 21.0 = 34.0 °C, so Q = 209 × 34.0 = 7,106 J.
You left out the mass of the water (4.18 × 34.0). Include m = 50 g: 50 × 4.18 × 34.0 = 7,106 J.
You used the starting temperature (21.0 °C) instead of the change. ΔT = 34.0 °C, so Q = 7,106 J.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains why the walnut sample heated the water much more than the popcorn sample?
options: The walnut is high in fat, and fat stores more energy per gram than carbohydrate does.
The walnut sample had a greater mass than the popcorn sample.
The water under the walnut started at a much higher temperature.
Popcorn is high in fat, and fat stores less energy per gram than carbohydrate does.
items.explain:
The walnut raised the water 40.0 °C; the popcorn raised it only 15.0 °C. The passage says walnuts are high in fat and popcorn is mostly carbohydrate. Fat stores more energy per gram (about 9 Calories) than carbohydrate (about 4 Calories).

Both samples had the same mass (1.0 g). The starting temperatures were almost the same (21.0 and 22.0 °C), and the calculation uses the temperature change, not the starting value. Popcorn is mostly carbohydrate, not fat.
why: Both samples had the same mass, 1.0 g, so mass cannot explain the difference.
The starting temperatures were nearly the same (21.0 and 22.0 °C), and the energy depends on the change in temperature, not the start.
The passage says popcorn is made mostly of carbohydrate, not fat, and fat stores more energy per gram than carbohydrate, not less.

items.prompt: Nutrition data list about 5.9 Calories per gram for peanuts, which equals about 24,700 J per gram. The class measured far less energy than this for 1.0 g of peanut. What is the most likely reason?
options: Burning destroyed some of the energy stored in the peanut.
Much of the heat from the flame escaped into the air and the can instead of going into the water.
The water gave off energy to the peanut while the peanut was burning.
The peanut's chemical energy was changed into mass during burning.
items.explain:
Energy is conserved, but in an open setup much of the heat from the burning food warms the surrounding air and the metal can rather than the water. Only the heat that reaches the water is measured, so the result is much lower than the true energy content. (Some of the peanut may also not burn completely.)

Energy cannot be destroyed, so it was not lost from existence; it went somewhere that was not measured. Heat flows from the hot flame to the cooler water, not the reverse.
why: Energy cannot be destroyed. The missing energy went somewhere that was not measured, mostly into the air and the can.
Heat flows from the hot flame to the cooler water, not from the water back to the peanut.
Burning food does not change chemical energy into mass. The energy left as heat and light, much of which missed the water.

items.prompt:
Complete the statements.

When a food sample burns, {{0}} energy stored in the bonds of its molecules is changed mostly into {{1}} energy and light. As the water absorbs this energy, its molecules move {{2}}, and its temperature rises.

options: chemical
nuclear
elastic
sound
why: Nuclear energy is stored in the nuclei of atoms. Food stores energy in the bonds of its molecules: chemical energy.
Elastic energy is stored in stretched or compressed objects. Energy in molecular bonds is chemical energy.
Sound is energy of vibrations, not energy stored in molecular bonds. Food stores chemical energy.

options: electrical
thermal
chemical
magnetic
why: Burning does not produce electricity. It releases mostly thermal energy (heat) and some light.
Chemical energy is what the food starts with; burning changes it into thermal energy.
Burning does not produce magnetic energy. It releases heat and light.

options: more slowly
faster
closer to a stop
in a fixed position
why: Absorbing energy makes molecules move faster, not slower. Slower molecules would mean a lower temperature.
Molecules closer to a stop would mean a falling temperature. The water's temperature rises, so its molecules move faster.
Molecules in a fixed position describe a solid, not water gaining heat. Absorbing energy makes them move faster.

items.explain:
Food stores chemical energy in the bonds of its molecules. Burning releases it mostly as thermal energy (heat) and some light.

Temperature measures the average motion of particles. When the water absorbs thermal energy, its molecules move faster, so its temperature rises. Slower-moving molecules would mean a lower temperature.

items.prompt:
Magnesium hydroxide, the active ingredient in Brand Y, reacts with hydrochloric acid to form magnesium chloride and water. Choose the coefficients that balance the equation.

Mg(OH)2 + {{0}} HCl → MgCl2 + {{1}} H2O

why: With 1 HCl, the left side has 1 chlorine atom but MgCl<sub>2</sub> has 2. Use 2 HCl.
3 HCl gives 3 chlorine atoms on the left but only 2 on the right. Use 2.
4 HCl gives 4 chlorine atoms on the left but only 2 on the right. Use 2.
With 1 H<sub>2</sub>O, the right side has 1 oxygen atom but Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> has 2. Use 2 H<sub>2</sub>O.
3 H<sub>2</sub>O gives 3 oxygen atoms on the right but only 2 on the left. Use 2.
4 H<sub>2</sub>O gives 4 oxygen atoms on the right but only 2 on the left. Use 2.

items.explain:
MgCl2 has 2 chlorine atoms, so the left side needs 2 HCl.

Mg(OH)2 has 2 oxygen atoms, so the right side needs 2 H2O.

Check: Left: 1 Mg, 2 O, 2 + 2 = 4 H, 2 Cl. Right: 1 Mg, 2 Cl, 2 O, 4 H. Balanced. Using 1 HCl would leave only 1 Cl on the left but 2 on the right.

items.prompt: Based on the results, which brand neutralized the most acid per gram of tablet?
options: Brand Z, because its final pH was the lowest
Brand X, because its final pH was in the middle
All three brands neutralized the same amount, because each beaker started at pH 1.5
Brand Y, because it raised the pH the most, closest to neutral
items.explain:
Each beaker started at pH 1.5 with the same acid and received the same mass of antacid. The brand that moved the pH furthest toward 7 neutralized the most acid. Brand Y raised the pH to 6.8, the closest to neutral.

Brand Z's low final pH (2.2) means the most acid was left over, so it neutralized the least. The different final pH values show the brands were not equally effective.
why: A low final pH means more acid was left, so Brand Z neutralized the least, not the most.
Brand X raised the pH to 3.5, but Brand Y raised it to 6.8, much closer to neutral.
All beakers started at pH 1.5, but the final pH values differ (2.2, 3.5, 6.8), so the brands did not neutralize the same amount.

items.prompt: The acid started at pH 1.5. After Brand X was added, the pH was 3.5. The starting acid was how many times more acidic than the solution after Brand X was added? Enter a whole number.
items.explain:
The pH changed by 3.5 − 1.5 = 2 units.

Each pH unit is a factor of 10, so 2 units = 10 × 10 = 100 times.

A common error is answering 2 (just the difference in pH) or 20 (2 × 10). The pH scale is logarithmic, so the factors of 10 multiply.

mistakes.why: 2 is the change in pH units. Each unit is a factor of 10, so 2 units means 10 × 10 = 100 times.
You multiplied 2 × 10. The factors of 10 multiply for each unit: 10 × 10 = 100.
10 is the factor for one pH unit. The pH changed by 2 units, so 10 × 10 = 100.

items.prompt: Which hypothesis was the class most likely testing?
options: Taller buildings sway more than shorter buildings during an earthquake.
Buildings made of wood sway less than buildings made of steel.
Placing a building on rubber pads reduces how much its top floor sways during shaking.
Shaking a building for a longer time makes it sway more.
items.explain:
The only difference between Model A and Model B was the rubber pads, and the class measured how much each top floor swayed. So the hypothesis is that rubber pads reduce sway.

Both models were the same height and material, and every run lasted 20 seconds, so the experiment cannot test height, material, or shaking time.
why: Both models were the same height (four stories), so the experiment cannot test height.
Both models were made of the same wood and glue, and no steel model was tested.
Every run lasted 20 seconds, so shaking time was not varied.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the data?
options: At every shaking level, Model B's top floor swayed about half as much as Model A's, or less.
The rubber pads stopped Model B from swaying at all.
The rubber pads reduced sway only at the high shaking level.
Both models swayed less as the shaking became stronger.
items.explain:
Compare B to A at each level:

Low: 0.6 ÷ 1.2 = 0.50
Medium: 1.1 ÷ 2.5 = 0.44
High: 2.0 ÷ 4.4 ≈ 0.45

At every level, Model B swayed about half as much as Model A, or less.

Model B still swayed (0.6 to 2.0 cm), so the pads did not stop sway. The pads helped at all three levels, not only at high shaking. Both models swayed more, not less, as shaking increased.
why: Model B still swayed 0.6 to 2.0 cm, so the pads did not stop sway completely.
Model B swayed less at all three levels (0.6 vs. 1.2, 1.1 vs. 2.5, 2.0 vs. 4.4), not only at high shaking.
Both models swayed more, not less, as shaking increased: Model A went from 1.2 to 4.4 cm.

items.prompt:
Which changes would make the class's results more reliable?

Select two answers.
options: Run more trials at each shaking level
Build and test several more identical pairs of models
Make Model B taller than Model A
Shake Model A harder than Model B
Measure sway at the bottom floor only, where movement is smallest
items.explain:
Reliability improves with more repeated trials and more test subjects (more pairs of models), because random errors average out and one unusual model cannot decide the result.

Making the models different heights or shaking them differently would add a second changing variable, making it impossible to tell whether the pads caused the difference. Measuring only the bottom floor would ignore the sway the class set out to study.
why: Making the models different heights adds a second changing variable, so the class could not tell whether the pads or the height caused the difference.
Shaking the models differently adds a second variable; the shaking must be the same for a fair test.
Measuring only the bottom floor ignores the top-floor sway the class set out to compare and does not make results more repeatable.

items.prompt: P waves are compressional (longitudinal) waves. S waves are shear (transverse) waves. Drag each description to the type of seismic wave it describes.
choices: Arrive first at a seismic station
Push and pull rock back and forth in the same direction the wave travels
Move rock side to side, perpendicular to the direction the wave travels
Can travel through solids, liquids, and gases
items.explain:
P waves are the fastest, so they arrive first. As compressional (longitudinal) waves, they push and pull material in the same direction the wave travels, and they can move through solids, liquids, and gases.

S waves are transverse: they move rock side to side, perpendicular to the wave's direction. Liquids cannot resist this kind of sideways shearing, so S waves cannot travel through liquids. (This is how scientists learned that Earth's outer core is liquid.)
items.why: The most common error is putting "Can travel through solids, liquids, and gases" under S waves. Only P waves (compressional) travel through liquids; S waves move rock side to side, and liquids cannot carry that shearing motion.

items.prompt: The platform of a shake table has a mass of 40 kg. At one moment, the motor gives it an acceleration of 2.5 m/s2. Using F = ma, what net force is acting on the platform at that moment?
items.explain:
F = m × a
F = 40 kg × 2.5 m/s2 = 100 N

16 N comes from dividing 40 by 2.5. 42.5 N comes from adding mass and acceleration, and 37.5 N from subtracting them; force is mass times acceleration.
why: You divided mass by acceleration (40 ÷ 2.5). Newton's second law multiplies: F = 40 × 2.5 = 100 N.
You subtracted acceleration from mass. Force is mass times acceleration: 40 × 2.5 = 100 N.
You added mass and acceleration. Force is their product: 40 × 2.5 = 100 N.

items.prompt: One food Calorie equals 4,184 joules. A banana supplies about 105 Calories. About how many joules of energy does the banana supply?
items.explain:
Multiply Calories by the number of joules in one Calorie.

105 × 4,184 = 439,320 J

25 J comes from dividing 105 by 4.184. Because a joule is a much smaller unit than a Calorie, the number of joules must be much larger, so multiply. 4,289 J comes from adding. 4,393,200 J has an extra factor of 10.
why: You divided 105 by 4.184. A joule is much smaller than a Calorie, so the number of joules must be larger: multiply 105 × 4,184.
You added 105 and 4,184. Each of the 105 Calories equals 4,184 J, so multiply: 439,320 J.
You have an extra factor of 10. 105 × 4,184 = 439,320 J.

items.prompt: During an earthquake, a 2 kg vase falls from a shelf and is moving at 4 m/s just before it hits the floor. Kinetic energy is found with KE = ½mv2. What is the vase's kinetic energy just before it hits the floor?
options: 4 J
8 J
items.explain:
KE = ½ × m × v2
v2 = 4 × 4 = 16
KE = ½ × 2 × 16 = 16 J

32 J leaves out the ½. 4 J forgets to square the speed (½ × 2 × 4), and 8 J multiplies mass by speed (2 × 4) without squaring or halving.
why: You forgot to square the speed: ½ × 2 × 4 = 4. Square first: 4<sup>2</sup> = 16, so KE = ½ × 2 × 16 = 16 J.
You multiplied mass by speed (2 × 4) without squaring or halving. Use KE = ½ × 2 × 16 = 16 J.
You left out the ½: 2 × 16 = 32. KE = ½mv<sup>2</sup> = 16 J.

items.prompt: Using the rule in the passage, how far was Station South from the earthquake? Enter your answer in kilometers.
items.explain:
S–P lag time at Station South: 10:16:10 − 10:15:35 = 35 seconds.

Distance = 6 × 35 = 210 km.

Check: P waves cover 210 km in 210 ÷ 6 = 35 s, and S waves in 210 ÷ 3 = 70 s; the difference is 35 s. A common error is subtracting only the seconds digits (10 − 35) without accounting for the change from 10:15 to 10:16.

mistakes.why: You subtracted only the seconds and treated 10 − 35 as 25 s. From 10:15:35 to 10:16:10 is 35 seconds, so distance = 6 × 35 = 210 km.
35 is the S–P lag time in seconds, not the distance. Multiply by 6: 6 × 35 = 210 km.
You multiplied the lag by 3 (the S-wave speed). The passage's rule is distance = 6 × lag time: 6 × 35 = 210 km.

items.prompt: Which station was closest to the earthquake?
options: North
East
South
West
items.explain:
The closest station has the shortest S–P lag time.

North: 20 s (120 km)
East: 10 s (60 km)
South: 35 s (210 km)
West: 25 s (150 km)

East had the shortest lag, so it was closest. South had the longest lag and was the farthest.
why: North's S–P lag is 20 s (120 km), longer than East's 10 s, so North is farther away.
South has the longest lag, 35 s (210 km), so it was the farthest, not the closest.
West's lag is 25 s (150 km), longer than East's 10 s, so West is farther away.

items.prompt: Each station can determine only its distance from the earthquake, not the direction. Why do scientists need data from at least three stations to find the earthquake's location on a map?
options: Each station measures the earthquake's magnitude, and three magnitudes must be averaged.
P waves reach only one station, and S waves reach only two.
Three stations are needed to measure the time the earthquake began.
A distance from one station gives a circle of possible locations; three circles meet at only one point.
items.explain:
Knowing only a distance means the earthquake could be anywhere on a circle around that station. Two circles usually cross at two points, so the location is still uncertain. A third circle crosses only one of those points, pinning down the single location. This method is called triangulation.

Magnitude is not used to find location, all stations recorded both P and S waves, and the lag-time method finds distance without knowing the start time.
why: Magnitude describes size, not location; it is not averaged to find where the earthquake happened.
The table shows every station recorded both P and S waves.
The lag-time method finds distance without knowing when the earthquake began; the stations are needed to narrow down location.

items.prompt: A magnitude 6.0 earthquake and a magnitude 4.0 earthquake are recorded at the same distance. How many times greater is the wave amplitude of the magnitude 6.0 earthquake?
options: 2 times
10 times
20 times
100 times
items.explain:
The magnitudes differ by 6.0 − 4.0 = 2.0.

Each increase of 1.0 multiplies amplitude by 10, so 2.0 means 10 × 10 = 100 times.

2 times is just the difference in magnitude. 20 times multiplies 2 × 10 instead of 10 × 10. 10 times counts only one step.
why: 2 is just the difference in magnitude. Each step multiplies amplitude by 10, so 2 steps give 10 × 10 = 100.
10 times counts only one step. The magnitudes differ by 2.0, so multiply by 10 twice: 100.
You multiplied 2 × 10. Each step is a factor of 10, so two steps give 10 × 10 = 100.

items.prompt: About how many times more energy does a magnitude 7.0 earthquake release than a magnitude 5.0 earthquake?
options: About 64 times
About 1,000 times
About 10,000 times
About 32,000 times
items.explain:
The magnitudes differ by 2.0. Energy grows about 32 times for each 1.0 step.

32 × 32 = 1,024, or about 1,000 times.

64 times adds the factors (32 + 32) instead of multiplying them. 32,000 times multiplies by 1,000 instead of 32 for the second step. 10,000 times treats the energy factor as 100 per step.
why: You added the factors (32 + 32). Each step multiplies energy by 32: 32 × 32 ≈ 1,000.
You used a factor of 100 per step (100 × 100). Energy grows about 32 times per step: 32 × 32 ≈ 1,000.
You multiplied by 1,000 for the second step instead of 32. Two steps give 32 × 32 ≈ 1,000.

items.prompt: Four buildings are the same distance from an expected earthquake. Based on the passage, which building faces the greatest risk of damage from liquefaction?
options: A building on loose, water-soaked sand on filled land beside a harbor
A building on solid granite bedrock on a hillside
A building on dry, tightly packed soil far from any water
A building on a concrete slab poured directly onto bedrock
items.explain:
The passage says liquefaction happens when loose, sandy soil is soaked with water and shaken. Filled land beside a harbor with water-soaked sand matches every condition.

The passage states that firm bedrock and dry, tightly packed soil do not liquefy, so the other three sites are not at risk from liquefaction (though they may still shake).
why: The passage says firm bedrock does not liquefy, so a building on granite bedrock is not at risk from liquefaction.
The passage says dry, tightly packed soil does not liquefy.
A slab poured onto bedrock rests on firm rock, which the passage says does not liquefy.
